summary: Australia's Guantánamo Bay prisoner David Hicks pleaded guilty to providing material support to the Taliban and was sentenced by a military commission to seven years but will serve only nine months, most of it in Australia, under a plea agreement that requires his transfer to Australia within 60 days and bars him for one year from speaking to the media, suing the U.S. government, appealing his sentence or profiting from selling his story. Michael Ratner, president of the Center for Constitutional Rights, called the restrictions a "modern cutting out of his tongue," while Hicks's father Terry Hicks said he was glad his son was returning home. Prosecutor Marine Lt. Col. Kevin Chenail, referring to Hicks as "Muhammad Dawood," urged the maximum sentence saying "we are on the front lines of the global war on terror... The enemy is sitting at the defense table," and Australian Greens Senator Bob Brown accused the restrictions of being a deliberate attempt to influence upcoming elections, a charge Prime Minister John Howard rejected as "absurd," saying the sentence was imposed by the military commission and worked out between the military prosecution and Hicks's lawyers.
